content:
Mathlib PR #38956 (just some renaming) broke a proof in FLT. I took a look and it looked like this:

The warning on S.linearProjOfIsCompl is 

`Submodule.linearProjOfIsCompl` has been deprecated: Use `Submodule.projectionOnto` instead

The mathlib PR has

@[deprecated (since := "2026-05-04")] alias linearProjOfIsCompl := projectionOnto

I changed the two occurrences of linearProjOfIsCompl to projectionOnto and simp_all worked again.

I just wondered if that was expected. It didn't cause me any trouble, everything was trivial to fix here, but it just made me wonder whether deprecations should be abbrevs.
This probably means that simp was removed from the deprecated lemmas
@Kevin Buzzard what tool are you using to find the exact PR that broke the proof?
Well, in this case you're just looking for the PR adding the deprecation, so you can git blame the alias, no?
Off-topic, but I'm a guinea-pig for an experimental tool -- see FLT#943 and FLT#944 (which I'm sure people could get excited about but then my question will be lost)
(See #mathlib4 > hopscotch-action: auto-bump mathlib, detect breaking changes.)
(it's really really really good BTW, it is constantly a time-saver)

Eric Wieser said:

This probably means that simp was removed from the deprecated lemmas

Yes that's it. I went back and squeezed the simps. linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left used to be a simp lemma and used to be about linearProjOfIsCompl. Then linearProjOfIsCompl was renamed to projectionOnto and both linearProjOfIsCompl and linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left were deprecated (the latter to projectionOnto_apply_left). However just making linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left into a simp lemma doesn't make the proof work again, because even though it's called linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left it's now a theorem about projectionOnto. So the "fix" (if one even needs a fix) isn't to inherit tags like simp on deprecated theorems, it's to make the deprecated definitions more transparent.

I'm not pushing for a change here, it was just a curiosity.

Kevin Buzzard said:

However just making linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left into a simp lemma doesn't make the proof work again, because even though it's called linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left it's now a theorem about projectionOnto.

This should have been caught on review; the statement of deprecated theorems shouldn't be changed

Maybe there's a meta-question here; is @[deprecated] supposed to keep downstream code working, or do we only really care about ensuring we provide clear instructions on how to fix it, such that breaking code is fine?

In the past I've seen contributors do the right thing, but then get confused by the warning along the lines of "warning in linearProjOfIsCompl_apply_left: linearProjOfIsCompl is deprecated", and so then they break the statement to make lean go away instead of telling Lean to silence the warning.

Yes, the meta-question was why I raised the issue. In practice here it was extremely easy to fix, I only mentioned it at all because I'd never seen this phenomenon before. Usually when things break after a rename it's because deprecations have been done incorrectly (or not done at all), whereas here I think there's a case for arguing that sometimes a "perfect deprecation" is not feasible and it's entirely reasonable to have a "best effort deprecation", as I think we can argue here was what happened.

This should have been caught on review; the statement of deprecated theorems shouldn't be changed

Thinking about it more, I think that this might be quite a lot to ask contributors and we'd be better off pushing for a tool which does all deprecations in a perfect or close-to-perfect way.
You're correct that using abbrev would likely decrease the chance of this kind of trouble

FWIW the deprecated-in-deprecated fix was merged today so this specific issue might be fine in the future, but might I suggest a different one:
When renaming IsFoo to IsBar, should one add deprecations for stuff under the renamed namespace? e.g. is it okay to rename IsFoo.baz → IsBar.baz without a deprecation, since downstream code will get a warning on the namespace already?

Snir Broshi said:

since downstream code will get a warning on the namespace already?

Is this so?

@[deprecated]
abbrev BadNat := Nat

def BadNat.foo : BadNat := 1

#check BadNat.foo -- no warning
Because #check is silly

import Mathlib
def IsBar (n : Nat) : Prop := n = 37
@[deprecated (since := "today")] alias IsFoo := IsBar
theorem IsBar.eq {n : Nat} (h : IsBar n) : n = 37 := h

/--
warning: `IsFoo` has been deprecated: Use `IsBar` instead
---
error: Unknown constant `IsFoo.eq`
-/
#guard_msgs in
theorem downstream_isFoo : 37 = 37 := by
  exact IsFoo.eq rfl -- even when not using the bare `IsFoo`, there's a warning

Snir Broshi said:

Because #check is silly

what does this mean?
since it's not related to #check
It doesn't show deprecations, you can delete the .foo in Eric's example and still not get a warning

but it's also not because of #check

-- warning: deprecation must specify date or version
@[deprecated]
abbrev BadNat := Nat

-- warning: `BadNat` is deprecated
def BadNat.foo : BadNat := 1

-- no warnings
theorem downstream_thm : True := by
  let := BadNat.foo
  trivial

Oh, apparently the issue is that BadNat.foo still exists. I still think there's an issue with #check, but it looks like the "Unknown constant" error triggers the deprecation error even inside #check, which is nice.
Regardless, my question stands. I've demonstrated that both methods lead to deprecation warnings downstream, the question is are we okay with the errors next to it?

Same problem goes to https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/38184#issuecomment-4582021011. Maybe we should make alias @[reducible, inline] (i.e. abbrev). The old alias has no problems on theorems (which is the usual use case) but creates weirdness on definitions.
